title: Pull one paper cup out of a wall cup dispenser, rim through the gasket, and stand it upright on the mat
instruction: Pull one paper cup out of the wall dispenser and stand it upright on the black mat.
context: Taking a paper cup from the dispenser by an office water cooler or coffee station is an everyday task. Only the bottom cup hangs out, held by its rolled rim on the dispenser's soft gasket with the next cups nested inside it: a robot has to reach it from the side under the dispenser, pinch the light, thin cup without crushing it, draw it straight down so its rim snaps through while the gasket keeps the next cup, and stand it upright.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left); heights above the counter (the table top). The layout is the same in every trial. (1) A wall: a white painted panel 2 thick, 80 wide (y -25 to 55) and 62 tall, its face at x 44.75. (2) On it, a stainless-steel pull-type cup dispenser for 8-24 oz cups (for example a San Jamar C3450SS): a vertical tube 11 across outside and 41 long, capped at the top, held 1.2 off the wall by two steel brackets; its axis at x 38, y 14; its bottom edge 15 above the counter. In its bottom end a black silicone gasket in a ring 10.6 across and 1.6 tall rests on a 3 mm lip; the gasket's eight flaps reach in to 8.5 across and give outward and downward when a cup's rim is pulled down through them, which takes a pull of about TBD N. (3) Four white 12 oz (355 ml) single-wall paper hot cups, 11 tall, 9 across the rolled rim and 6 across the bottom, 11 g each, nested 1.8 apart, open end up, inside the dispenser: the bottom one hangs by its rim on the gasket's flaps with its bottom 6 above the counter, so about 9 of it sticks out below the dispenser. (4) A black rubber bar mat, 16 (x) by 12 (y) and 4 mm thick, centred at x 34, y -3 (right of the dispenser), flat on the counter.
scoring: Judged with a tape measure and a protractor at the end, and from the trial video for what happens during it. A cup is out of the dispenser when all of it, rim included, is below the dispenser's bottom edge. A cup is still in the dispenser when it hangs upright (within 10 degrees) no more than 5 mm lower than the bottom cup hung at the start (its bottom 6 above the counter). 0 if two or more cups are out, or if any cup was crushed (squeezed hard enough to dent or crease it: in the video its wall visibly pushed in; in the sim a grip force over 20 N on it), ever tipped more than 60 degrees from upright (dropped or knocked over), or ends on the floor: such a cup would be thrown away. Otherwise 0.25 when exactly one cup is out. 0.5 when, also, every other cup is still in the dispenser and the cup that is out stands upright (within 10 degrees) with its bottom edge on the counter or the mat (within 6 mm), still (no visible movement for 1 s), with no part of either gripper within 1.5 cm of it. 1.0 when, also, its whole bottom is on the mat (its centre at least 3 cm inside every edge of the mat). The trial ends at the run limit, or when 1.0 has held for 1 s.
reset_notes: Each trial uses one cup. Take the cap off the dispenser, lift out the cups left in it, and drop a nested stack of four fresh cups in so the bottom one hangs by its rim on the gasket; put the cap back.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (Isaac Sim, PhysX, 20 Hz). The paper cups are rigid shells (24 facets, 1.2 mm walls, a hexagonal rolled rim) that can't dent, so crushing is scored from grip force (finger position error x 5,000 N/m; over 20 N counts). Nested cups sit 1.8 cm apart on four small bumps and don't stick. The gasket is eight sprung flaps (60 N/m each) sliding outward and down at 45 degrees. Four cups instead of a full sleeve. Friction: cup 0.6, silicone 0.7.
